items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1959-06-30
items.q: He reminded me of George Lewis.

ctx.x: Who was involved with the Blues band? Do you remember any of those guys?

Yeah, Amelia Barnes was in the band. Amelia Barnes, an old man played with a six-string banjo. Run over the lake and he died. He's on that Pitch and Esquire book with Buddy Petit. Yeah, I know what you mean. Buddy Manatee. And Israel, Israel Gorman. For years I could never get anybody to explain who he was, so I met him on the end of the union when I was there a few years back in the morning. He reminded me of George Lewis. I'd always tell Paul what happened to him. And he still acted. You ever seen him? Gabriel…

items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: If you play like George Lewis, he was never considered a great clarinet player. He got famous after Bunk Johnson picked him up...

ctx.x: How did he sound? There’s not much . . . George Boyd never recorded.

No. They all had that sound of bending notes, playing the blues and all, but they all played in tune. They never deviated from playing some other notes or bending a note wrong. They played within the context of the music. That’s what’s got to be watched when you’re playing a clarinet. You got to play that [expletive deleted] in tune, because it reflects. You got a problem on a note, [? (inaudible)] if you know it, but you got to play that clarinet in tune. If you play like George Lewis, he was never considered a…

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: Yeah, George Lewis, the clarinet player. Well, Bunk Johnson picked up this band...

ctx.x: Yeah, George Lewis, the clarinet player. Well, Bunk Johnson picked up this band, and they played a sort of...I don't know... A strange beat. A slower time New Orleans beat. You know, they wasn't too proficient on them instrument, so they played a certain tempo. You know, they never went into nothin' like no "Chinatown or none of them things -- or "Limehouse Blues."
